# Welcome {.unnumbered}

This book is a hands-on introduction to three closely related tools for
analysing health (and other) data in R:

1. **Kaplan–Meier curves**, which describe how survival changes over time
   and compare groups.
2. **Cox proportional hazards regression**, which models the effect of
   several variables on the hazard of an event.
3. **Propensity score matching**, which helps you estimate treatment effects
   from *observational* data, where treatment wasn't randomised.

The last chapter combines them. It takes an observational cohort, matches
treated and untreated patients on their propensity scores, and then
estimates the treatment effect on survival with Kaplan–Meier and Cox models.

## The big picture {.unnumbered}

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: "How the chapters fit together. Chapters 1–3 describe and model survival, and Chapter 4 covers three common traps. Chapters 5–6 deal with confounding in observational data. Chapter 7 then uses the Chapter 2–3 methods (dotted arrows) on the matched data."
flowchart LR
  A["<b>Ch 1</b><br/>Time-to-event data<br/>and censoring"] --> B["<b>Ch 2</b><br/>Describe and compare:<br/>Kaplan–Meier curves,<br/>log-rank test"]
  B --> C["<b>Ch 3</b><br/>Measure and adjust:<br/>Cox regression,<br/>hazard ratios"]
  C --> T["<b>Ch 4</b><br/>Common traps:<br/>censoring, competing<br/>events, time zero"]
  D["Observational data:<br/>treatment not<br/>randomised"] --> E["<b>Ch 5</b><br/>Confounding and<br/>propensity scores"]
  T --> E
  E --> G["<b>Ch 6</b><br/>Matching in R:<br/>MatchIt and<br/>balance checks"]
  G --> F["<b>Ch 7</b><br/>Matched analysis:<br/>KM and Cox on<br/>the matched data"]
  B -.-> F
  C -.-> F
```

- **Kaplan–Meier curves** *describe* survival over time, and the
  **log-rank test** asks whether groups differ.
- **Cox regression** *measures* how much groups differ (a hazard ratio) and
  can *adjust* for other variables.
- When treatment wasn't randomised, treated and untreated patients may
  differ in ways that also affect survival (**confounding**). **Propensity
  score matching** creates comparable groups first. Then the same KM and Cox
  methods are used on the matched data.

## How to use this book {.unnumbered}

Each chapter mixes three things:

- **Concepts.** Short explanations of what a method does and why.
- **R code.** Worked examples you can copy, and live exercises you run in the page. Each chapter builds on the last.
- **Interactive apps.** Small simulations that run in your browser. Change
  the sliders to see how a method behaves. Because the data are simulated,
  *we know the true answer* and can see when a method gets it right or wrong.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Start here
If you're new to these topics, read **[Before you start](00-before-you-start.qmd)**
first. It lists what the book assumes, with short refreshers. It also shows
how to set up R and download the course files, and explains what each type
of box in the book is for. Unfamiliar terms are defined in the
[Glossary](a2-glossary.qmd).
:::

The interactive apps **and the R exercises** run in your web browser, so
you don't need to install anything to work through the book. Each exercise
is a live code box where you write R, run it, and get instant feedback. Chapter 8 (@sec-shiny) describes two extra **Shiny apps** that
you download and run in RStudio.

::: {.callout-note}
## The data used in this book
- `survival::lung`: survival of 228 patients with advanced lung cancer
  (NCCTG). This dataset comes with the survival package and is used in
  Chapters 1–3. One exercise and Chapter 8 also use `survival::veteran`, a
  lung cancer trial. Chapter 4 uses three more datasets from the survival
  package: `mgus2` (a blood condition that can progress to cancer) and the
  Stanford heart transplant data (`jasa` and `heart`).
- A **simulated observational cohort** (@sec-cohort). Treatment is given
  more often to sicker patients, so a naive comparison is misleading. The
  true treatment effect is known (HR = 0.70). It is used in Chapters 5–7,
  and you can [download the script](R/simulate_cohort.R){download="simulate_cohort.R"}
  that creates it.
:::

## A suggested route {.unnumbered}

The core material (skipping the "Going further" boxes) fits into six
sessions of about 2 hours:

| Session | Chapters | Topics |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Before you start, 1, 2 | Survival data and censoring, Kaplan–Meier curves, the log-rank test |
| 2 | 3 | Hazards, Cox regression, checking proportional hazards |
| 3 | 4 (traps 1–2) | Informative censoring and competing risks |
| 4 | 4 (trap 3) | Immortal time bias, time-varying covariates, Exercise 4.1 |
| 5 | 5 | Confounding, propensity scores, matching by hand |
| 6 | 6, 7 | Matching in R and checking balance, then a complete matched survival analysis |

Chapter 8's Shiny apps are for open-ended practice after the sessions.
Chapters 9–11, in the **Going further** part, cover weighting and other
matching methods, what to do when proportional hazards fail, and missing
data. Read them when your own analysis needs them.
